speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the blood work results; since those are normal, I need to focus on the neurological aspect. Given your double vision and limb weakness, have you noticed any specific muscle wasting, weakness in swallowing, or changes in your speech pattern?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: The pattern of symptoms worsening with activity and improving with rest, along with your double vision upon looking up or down, is highly suggestive of a specific neuromuscular condition. Have you noticed any recent issues with your eyelids drooping or your speech becoming slurred?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is helpful; the absence of infection history and symmetrical weakness helps rule out other causes. Given the classic pattern of symptoms worsening with activity and improving with rest, along with your diplopia, do you have any difficulty with tasks that require fine motor skills, like holding a pen or buttoning a shirt?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had trouble swallowing or slurred speech. I also have not noticed breathing difficulty, and the symptoms started gradually about a month ago.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. The combination of fluctuating muscle weakness worsening with activity (fatigability), ptosis, diplopia (especially with up/down gaze), and proximal limb weakness, in the absence of other systemic signs like fever or infection, is highly characteristic of this autoimmune neuromuscular disorder.
